title: Android rebuild — the five decisions before the work starts

steps.path: Chat on the phone — what answers when you send a message
steps.headline: What should the phone run: the built-in assistant, a newer Claude Code, or both?
steps.today: On the phone every conversation is a Claude Code terminal session. The phone's copy of Claude Code is frozen at a version from spring because newer versions ship in a form the phone's runtime cannot start. Desktop always gets the newest version, and also has its own built-in assistant that talks to ChatGPT, OpenRouter and local models.
steps.problem: The phone falls further behind every day, shows commands its Claude Code does not have, and cannot use ChatGPT or OpenRouter at all. Unfreezing Claude Code on the phone is a runtime rework of unknown size; bringing the built-in assistant over is a known 3-to-5-week port.
steps.proposal: Pick what the rebuild leads with. Either way the phone keeps a working chat throughout.

options.label: Built-in assistant first
pros: ChatGPT and OpenRouter on the phone in weeks, the same behaviour as desktop.
The frozen Claude Code stays available as it is today, labelled as the older option.
cons: Claude Code on the phone stays at the spring version until someone takes on the runtime rework.
Two ways to chat on the phone, one of them visibly older.

options.label: Unfreeze Claude Code first
pros: The one thing the phone does today gets current and stays current.
cons: Unknown size: it means teaching the phone runtime to start a native program it cannot start today.
Still no ChatGPT or OpenRouter until the built-in assistant follows.

options.label: Built-in first, then unfreeze
cons: The longest path; the second half may never get scheduled.

steps.headline: Which comes first: the built-in assistant, or the phone basics?
steps.today: The phone is missing two different kinds of thing. One is the built-in assistant (ChatGPT, OpenRouter). The other is ordinary phone behaviour: notifications that arrive, sharing into the app from other apps, access to your real folders, an update check, a proper first-launch screen.
steps.problem: Both are weeks of work and they do not overlap much. Whichever goes second is what testers will complain about in the meantime.
steps.proposal: Pick the order. Small fixes that make the current app honest (real version numbers, notification permission, clean refusals) happen first regardless.

options.label: Built-in assistant first
pros: The biggest gap closes first; the phone becomes the same product as desktop.
The first-launch screen needs the assistant's sign-in anyway, so it is designed once.
cons: Notifications, sharing and file access stay missing for another month or so.

options.label: Phone basics first
pros: The app feels like a real phone app sooner: approval prompts arrive, you can share a screenshot into it.
cons: It is still a Claude Code-only app during that time, and the first-launch screen gets designed before the assistant it should introduce.

steps.page: How it ships and what it keeps
steps.intro: The first page decided what the phone runs. These decide how people get it and how much of the desktop's file features it carries.

steps.headline: Google Play, or keep the GitHub download with an in-app update check?
steps.today: The app is downloaded from GitHub as a file and installed by hand, with the security warnings that brings. There is no update check inside the app, so nobody finds out a newer build exists.
steps.problem: Most installed copies will quietly rot. A Play listing needs the company's identity paperwork, a data-safety form, a content rating, a slightly newer Android target and a first-launch consent screen; from 2027 Google requires a verified developer even for hand-installed apps.
steps.proposal: Pick the destination. The website's Android notice already says we are aiming for Google Play.

options.label: Google Play
pros: Installs and updates like every other app; no security warnings, no hunting for files.
Testing tracks let a few people try builds before everyone.
cons: Store-readiness work and paperwork before the first listing; Google reviews each release.
Google's rules on downloaded code may constrain how the phone runs Claude Code.

options.label: GitHub download plus an in-app update check
pros: Nothing to file; ships whenever we like.
The update check alone fixes the rot.
cons: Every install and update keeps the unknown-source warnings.
Runs into Google's 2027 developer-verification rule anyway.

options.label: Both
pros: Play for most people, GitHub for anyone who wants it.
cons: Two distribution paths to keep in step.

steps.headline: How much of the desktop's file features should the phone get?
steps.today: On desktop, Files shows every file in a project, lets you import, rename, exclude and delete, search inside files, and shows git changes. On the phone only the files a conversation produced are listed; everything else answers "not available".
steps.problem: The full file view is a large port on its own, and a phone screen is a poor place for a git surface. But a phone that cannot browse a project's files is a thinner product than the website claims.
steps.proposal: Pick the scope for the rebuild's first release.

options.label: Conversation files only
pros: Already works; the rebuild spends its time elsewhere.
The screens that cannot work on the phone are hidden cleanly instead of failing.
cons: No browsing a project's folder, no import, no git on the phone.

options.label: Browse and import, no git
pros: You can open any file in the project and add one from the phone.
cons: A few more weeks of phone work; live refresh and content search are extra on top.

options.label: Everything desktop has
cons: The largest option by far, and git on a phone screen has no design yet.

steps.headline: Should the phone keep its old restore-from-backup wizard, which desktop no longer has?
steps.today: In July desktop replaced its Google Drive and GitHub backup system with the current Sync Spaces design and deleted the restore wizard. The phone still runs the old system: it backs up to Drive and can restore from a dated snapshot. Nothing else in the product can read those backups any more.
steps.problem: It is the only place restore still exists, it does not talk to the current sync, and it is a chunk of phone-only code that the rebuild would otherwise delete.
steps.proposal: Yes removes it on the phone so both platforms match, and the phone gets the current sync when the built-in assistant's runtime arrives. No keeps it until then. Don't know leaves it in place for now.
